macau.s: Macau is a territory on the south coast of China, at the mouth of the Pearl River. The Portuguese established a settlement there in the sixteenth century, making it an important hub for trade between China, Japan and Europe.

maccabean-revolt.s: The Maccabean Revolt was a Jewish uprising against the Seleucid Empire lasting from 167 to 142 BCE, provoked by the religious policies of Antiochus IV. Led by the Maccabee family, the rebels rededicated the Temple in Jerusalem and eventually won independence.

macedonian-dynasty.s: The Macedonian dynasty ruled the Byzantine Empire from 867 to 1056, beginning with Basil I. Its era saw military recovery, territorial expansion and a cultural and legal revival.

macedonian-empire.s: The Macedonian Empire was the empire created by Alexander the Great, who conquered the Achaemenid Empire and reached as far as the Indus between 334 and 323 BCE. After his death it broke apart into the successor kingdoms, including the Ptolemaic and Seleucid empires.

macedonians-ethnic-group.s: The Macedonians, in the modern sense, are a South Slavic people of the region of Macedonia in the southern Balkans. In the late Ottoman Empire, Macedonia was a contested province where Bulgarian, Greek and Serbian nationalisms competed.

madeira.s: Madeira is an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of north-west Africa. Portuguese navigators settled it in the early fifteenth century, making it one of the first possessions of the Portuguese Empire.

madhab.s: A madhab is a school of Islamic jurisprudence, a tradition of legal interpretation based on the Quran and Sunna. The four main Sunni schools, the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafii and Hanbali, took shape during the Abbasid Caliphate.

madrasa.s: A madrasa is an Islamic institution of higher learning, typically teaching law, theology and related sciences. The Seljuk Empire, notably under the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, founded influential madrasas to train scholars and officials and promote Sunni orthodoxy.

madrid.s: Madrid is the capital of Spain, in the centre of the Iberian peninsula. Philip II made it the permanent seat of the royal court in 1561.

madurai.s: Madurai is an ancient city in southern India, the capital of the Pandya kingdom. In the early fourteenth century Malik Kafur, general of Alauddin Khalji of the Delhi Sultanate, sacked the Pandya treasury at Madurai.

magadha.s: Magadha was an ancient kingdom in the eastern Ganges plain, in present-day Bihar, with its capital at Pataliputra. It was the power base from which the Maurya Empire expanded across most of the Indian subcontinent.

magan.s: Magan was an ancient land known to Mesopotamian sources, generally identified with present-day Oman and adjacent coasts. It was a source of copper and stone reached by sea through the Persian Gulf.

maghreb.s: The Maghreb is the region of north-west Africa comprising present-day Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya. It was the heartland of the Almohad Caliphate, which unified it under one rule in the twelfth century.

magnates.s: Magnates were the great noble landowners of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, whose vast estates gave them enormous wealth and influence. Many maintained private armies and pursued their own political and military interests.

magnetic-compass.s: The magnetic compass is a navigational instrument that uses a magnetised needle to indicate direction. It was developed in China and was used for navigation at sea under the Song Dynasty, among the earliest recorded uses.

mago-agricultural-writer.s: Mago was a Carthaginian writer on agriculture who composed a large treatise on farming. The Punic Empire's profile states that the work, in twenty-eight volumes, was so highly regarded that the Roman Senate ordered its translation into Latin after Carthage's destruction in 146…

mago-i.s: Mago I was a Carthaginian leader of the sixth century BCE, active around 550 to 530 BCE, and founder of the Magonid dynasty. According to the Punic Empire's profile, he began the systematic empire-building that transformed Carthage from a trading post into an imperial metropolis.

magonid-dynasty.s: The Magonid dynasty was a leading family of Carthage, founded by Mago I in the sixth century BCE. Its members dominated Carthaginian politics and military command for generations.

magyars.s: The Magyars are the Hungarian people, who settled the Carpathian Basin in the late ninth century. Their raids troubled Germany and Italy until Otto I defeated them at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955.

mahamatra.s: Mahamatra was a title for senior officials in the Maurya Empire. According to the empire's profile, they served as provincial governors and officials responsible for collecting revenue, maintaining law and order and supervising public works.

maharajadhiraja.s: Maharajadhiraja, meaning 'great king of kings', was an Indian imperial title. Chandragupta I adopted it, marking the transition of the Gupta rulers from regional chieftains to imperial sovereigns.

mahatma-gandhi.s: Mahatma Gandhi was the leader of the Indian independence movement, known for his strategy of non-violent mass resistance. Campaigns such as the Salt March of 1930 and the Quit India movement of 1942 mobilised millions against British rule.

mahayana-buddhism.s: Mahayana Buddhism is a major branch of Buddhism emphasising the bodhisattva ideal and a broad body of scriptures. Srivijaya was an important centre of Mahayana learning, attracting pilgrims and scholars.

mahdi.s: The Mahdi, meaning 'the rightly guided one', is a figure in Islamic belief expected to appear to restore justice and true religion. Claims to be the Mahdi have legitimised several movements.

mahdist-state.s: The Mahdist State was the state founded in Sudan by Muhammad Ahmad, who proclaimed himself the Mahdi in 1881, and continued under his successor the Khalifa Abdallahi. Following al-Zubayr's defeat of the Darfur sultan in 1874, Darfur was absorbed by the Mahdists, extinguishing…

mahmud-hotak.s: Mahmud Hotak was an Afghan ruler of the Ghilzai Hotak dynasty, son of Mirwais Hotak. In 1722 he defeated the Safavid army at Gulnabad and besieged and captured Isfahan, forcing Shah Sultan Husayn to abdicate.

mahmud-iv.s: Mahmud IV was the last mansa of the Mali Empire. By his time the Keita dynasty controlled little beyond its Kangaba heartland.

mahmud-yalavach.s: Mahmud Yalavach was a Khwarazmian Muslim administrator in the service of the Mongol Empire. Appointed by the Great Khan, he governed the sedentary cities of Transoxiana during Chagatai's lifetime.

mai-title.s: Mai was the title of the kings of Kanem-Bornu, held by rulers of the Sayfawa dynasty. The mai held sacred and political authority and governed with a council of notables and royal officials.

maimonides.s: Maimonides was a Jewish philosopher, legal scholar and physician born in Cordoba in the twelfth century. His family left al-Andalus after the Almohad conquest imposed pressure on Jews and Christians, and he eventually settled in Egypt.

mainz.s: Mainz is a city on the Rhine in western Germany and one of the oldest episcopal seats north of the Alps. Its archbishop was one of the seven prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire and served as arch-chancellor of Germany.

maize.s: Maize is a cereal crop domesticated in Mesoamerica, the staple of the Aztec and other American civilisations. After the Spanish Empire's conquests it spread worldwide through the Columbian Exchange.

majapahit-empire.s: The Majapahit Empire was a Hindu-Buddhist maritime state based in eastern Java, founded in 1293 after the repulse of a Mongol expedition. Under the minister Gajah Mada and King Hayam Wuruk in the fourteenth century, it claimed authority across much of the Indonesian archipelago.

malabar-coast.s: The Malabar Coast is the south-western coast of India, in present-day Kerala and neighbouring areas, long famous for its pepper and spice trade. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on this coast in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to India.

malacca.s: Malacca is a port city on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, overlooking the Strait of Malacca. The Malacca Sultanate, founded around 1400, became the leading entrepot of South-East Asia after the decline of Srivijaya and Majapahit.

malatya.s: Malatya is a city in eastern Anatolia, on the upper Euphrates. After the collapse of the Hittite Empire, it was the centre of one of the Neo-Hittite states that preserved Hittite political and artistic traditions.

malay-language.s: The Malay language is an Austronesian language spoken in the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and much of maritime South-East Asia. Its earliest inscriptions, in Old Malay, date from the period of Srivijaya.

malay-peninsula.s: The Malay Peninsula is the long peninsula of South-East Asia extending south from mainland Asia between the Andaman Sea and the South China Sea. Its control of the Strait of Malacca made it strategically valuable to Srivijaya and later the Majapahit Empire.

malaya.s: Malaya was the name for British territories on the Malay Peninsula, comprising the Straits Settlements and the Malay states under British protection. It was valued for its tin and rubber.

malgum.s: Malgum was a minor Mesopotamian kingdom on the Tigris in the early second millennium BCE. It joined a coalition with Elam, Ashur, Eshnunna and others that confronted Hammurabi around 1764 BCE.

mali.s: Mali refers both to the medieval Mali Empire and to the region of the upper and middle Niger in West Africa, now the Republic of Mali. The area was a centre of trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt.

mali-conquest-of-koumbi-saleh.s: The Mali conquest of Koumbi Saleh in 1240 was the capture of the former capital of the Ghana Empire by the forces of Sundiata Keita. It followed Sundiata's victory over the Sosso at Kirina.

mali-empire.s: The Mali Empire was a West African empire founded by Sundiata Keita around 1235, which flourished until the fifteenth century. It controlled trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt and reached its height under Mansa Musa, whose pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 became famous.

malik-kafur.s: Malik Kafur was a general of Alauddin Khalji, sultan of Delhi, in the early fourteenth century. He led the sultanate's most spectacular campaigns into southern India, extracting tribute from the Hoysala kingdom and sacking the Pandya treasury at Madurai.

maliki-school.s: The Maliki school is one of the four Sunni schools of Islamic law, named after the jurist Malik ibn Anas of Medina. It became dominant in North and West Africa and al-Andalus.

malik-shah-i.s: Malik Shah I was sultan of the Seljuk Empire from 1072 until his death in 1092, when the empire reached its greatest extent. Assisted by his vizier Nizam al-Mulk, he presided over a period of strong administration and cultural flourishing.

mallam-dendo.s: Mallam Dendo was a Fulani scholar and one of the flag-bearers of Usman dan Fodio's jihad in the early nineteenth century. He led the movement in the Nupe region, where his descendants established the emirate of Bida.

maluku-islands.s: The Maluku Islands, or Moluccas, are an archipelago in eastern Indonesia, historically known as the Spice Islands. They were the original source of cloves, nutmeg and mace, which were highly prized in global trade.

malwa.s: Malwa is a region of west-central India, on a plateau north of the Narmada river. It was a fertile and strategically placed territory contested by successive powers.

mamluk.s: A mamluk was an enslaved soldier, usually of Turkic or Caucasian origin, bought and trained for military service in Islamic states. Mamluks became central to the armies of the Abbasid Caliphate and the Ayyubid Empire.

mamluk-dynasty-delhi.s: The Mamluk dynasty, also called the Slave Dynasty, was the first ruling line of the Delhi Sultanate, from 1206 to 1290. It was founded by Qutb al-Din Aibak, a former slave commander of Muhammad of Ghor.

mamluk-sultanate.s: The Mamluk Sultanate was a state ruled by mamluk soldier elites in Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517. It replaced the Ayyubid Empire and defeated the Mongols of the Ilkhanate at Ain Jalut in 1260, halting their advance.

manchu-han-dyarchy.s: The Manchu-Han dyarchy was the practice in the Qing Empire of appointing both a Manchu and a Han Chinese official to many senior posts. It allowed the Manchu ruling minority to share power with the Han majority while keeping overall control.

manchukuo.s: Manchukuo was a puppet state established by the Empire of Japan in Manchuria in 1932, after the Mukden Incident and the Japanese occupation of the region. It was nominally headed by Puyi, the last Qing emperor.

manchuria.s: Manchuria is a region of north-east China, bordering Korea and Russia. It was the homeland of the Manchus, who founded the Qing Empire and conquered China from there.

manchus.s: The Manchus are a people of north-east Asia descended from the Jurchens of Manchuria. United by Nurhaci and his successors, they founded the Qing Empire, which conquered Ming China from 1644.

mandala-political-model.s: The mandala political model is a scholarly concept describing states in pre-modern South-East Asia as circles of power radiating from a central ruler. Authority weakened with distance, and outlying rulers shifted allegiance among centres.

mandinka.s: The Mandinka are a West African people of the Mande group, living mainly in present-day Mali, Guinea, Senegal and the Gambia. Under Sundiata Keita, they founded the Mali Empire.

mani.s: Mani was a Persian prophet of the third century CE and founder of Manichaeism. According to the Aksumite Empire's profile, he described Aksum as one of the four great powers of the world, alongside Rome, Persia and China.

manichaeism.s: Manichaeism was a religion founded by the prophet Mani in the third century CE, teaching a dualism of light and darkness. It spread widely from the Roman world to China.

manikongo.s: Manikongo was the title of the king of the Kingdom of Kongo. The manikongo ruled from Mbanza Kongo over provinces such as Soyo, Mbata and Nsundi, governing through appointed officials and tribute.

manila.s: Manila is the capital of the Philippines, on Manila Bay in Luzon. The Spanish established it as the colonial capital of the Philippines in 1571.

manila-galleon.s: The Manila galleon was the Spanish trade route across the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco, in operation from 1565 to 1815. Galleons carried American silver to Asia and returned with Chinese silk, porcelain and other goods.

manilla.s: A manilla was a horseshoe-shaped bracelet of copper or brass used as currency in West Africa. Manillas were introduced in large quantities through European trade, especially by the Portuguese, and were used in the Atlantic slave trade.

manipular-legion.s: The manipular legion was the organisation of the Roman army of the middle Republic, in which the legion was divided into small, flexible units called maniples. This structure gave Roman armies greater tactical flexibility than the Macedonian phalanx.

manishtushu.s: Manishtushu was a king of the Akkadian Empire in the twenty-third century BCE, a son of Sargon of Akkad. He campaigned across the Persian Gulf and is known from an obelisk recording large land purchases.

mansa.s: Mansa was the title of the rulers of the Mali Empire, meaning king or emperor in the Mandinka language. The mansa held supreme political, military and religious authority.

mansa-musa.s: Mansa Musa was ruler of the Mali Empire from 1312 to 1337, under whom the empire reached its greatest wealth and extent. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, during which he distributed vast quantities of gold, made Mali famous across the Islamic world and Europe.

mansa-musas-pilgrimage.s: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage was the journey of the ruler of the Mali Empire to Mecca in 1324. Accompanied by a vast retinue, he distributed so much gold, notably in Cairo, that its value there is reported to have fallen.

mansa-sakura.s: Mansa Sakura was a ruler of the Mali Empire in the late thirteenth century, a former military commander who seized the throne. According to the empire's profile, his reign brought a military revival, extending Mali's reach north to the Niger bend and west towards the Atlantic.

mansa-uli.s: Mansa Uli was a son of Sundiata Keita and one of the early rulers of the Mali Empire. He expanded the empire towards the Senegal River.

mansabdari-system.s: The mansabdari system was the ranking system of the Mughal Empire, established under Akbar. Each official, or mansabdar, held a numerical rank determining his status, pay and the number of cavalry he had to maintain.

manshur.s: A manshur was a formal decree or diploma of investiture issued by a caliph. In 1229 the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir issued a manshur to Iltutmish, recognising him as sultan of the Delhi Sultanate.

manueline-style.s: The Manueline style is a Portuguese architectural style of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, named after King Manuel I. It combined late Gothic forms with elaborate maritime and exotic motifs such as ropes, shells and armillary spheres.

manuscript.s: A manuscript is a handwritten book or document. Manuscript traditions were central to learning and record-keeping in many empires, from the scholarly libraries of Timbuktu in the Songhai and Mali empires to illuminated works of the Ilkhanate and the Ottoman Empire.

manuscript-illumination.s: Manuscript illumination is the decoration of handwritten books with painted images, ornament and gold. Under the Ilkhanate, Persian illumination and painting absorbed Chinese influences, producing works such as illustrated histories and copies of the Shahnameh.

manyema.s: Manyema is a region of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, west of Lake Tanganyika. According to the Luba Empire's profile, Luba military expeditions extended north into Manyema during the empire's height.

mara-takla-haymanot.s: Mara Takla Haymanot was an Ethiopian ruler who founded the Zagwe dynasty. According to the Aksumite Empire's profile, he was a general who defeated the last Aksumite king, Dil Na'od, around 940 CE.

maragha.s: Maragha is a city in north-western Iran, in the region of Azerbaijan. It served as an early capital of the Ilkhanate under Hulagu.

maratha-confederacy.s: The Maratha Confederacy refers to the Maratha state in its later form, when power was shared among the Peshwa and great Maratha chiefs such as the Scindias, Holkars, Gaekwads and Bhonsles. In the eighteenth century it expanded rapidly at the expense of the Mughal Empire.

maratha-empire.s: The Maratha Empire was an Indian state founded by Shivaji in the seventeenth century in the western Deccan. Its long war against Aurangzeb drained the Mughal Empire, and in the eighteenth century the Marathas became the dominant power in much of India.

marathi.s: Marathi is an Indo-Aryan language spoken mainly in western India, in present-day Maharashtra. It was the language of the Maratha people and Shivaji promoted it in administration in place of Persian.

marcelo-caetano.s: Marcelo Caetano was the prime minister of Portugal from 1968 to 1974, succeeding Antonio Salazar as head of the authoritarian Estado Novo regime. He continued the costly colonial wars in Africa.

march-across-the-belts.s: The March across the Belts was a campaign in 1658 in which King Charles X Gustav of Sweden led his army across the frozen straits of Denmark. The surprise attack forced Denmark to accept the Treaty of Roskilde, ceding large territories to Sweden.

marco-polo.s: Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant and traveller who lived in China between 1275 and 1292 during the Yuan Dynasty. He served at the court of Kublai Khan and travelled widely in his realm.

marcus-licinius-crassus.s: Marcus Licinius Crassus was a wealthy Roman politician and general, a member of the First Triumvirate with Pompey and Julius Caesar. He invaded the Parthian Empire and was decisively defeated and killed at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE.

marduk.s: Marduk was the chief god of Babylon, elevated to head of the Mesopotamian pantheon as Babylon's power grew. His cult was central to the legitimacy of Babylonian kings under the Babylonian and Chaldean empires.

mare-nostrum.s: Mare Nostrum, meaning 'our sea', was the Roman name for the Mediterranean Sea. It expressed the fact that Rome controlled all the lands around it after defeating Carthage and the Hellenistic kingdoms.

margrave-of-brandenburg.s: The Margrave of Brandenburg was the ruler of the March of Brandenburg in north-eastern Germany. Under the Golden Bull of 1356 the margrave was one of the seven prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire.

mari.s: Mari was an ancient city on the middle Euphrates in present-day Syria, a major trading centre in the early second millennium BCE. Its palace archives are a key source for the diplomacy of the age, including relations between Babylon, Elam and other powers.

marinid-dynasty.s: The Marinid dynasty was a Berber dynasty that ruled Morocco from the mid-thirteenth to the fifteenth century. The Marinids rose as the Almohad Caliphate disintegrated and captured Marrakesh in 1269, ending Almohad rule.

mark-antony.s: Mark Antony was a Roman general and politician, an ally of Julius Caesar and later a member of the Second Triumvirate. His alliance and relationship with Cleopatra VII bound him to the Ptolemaic Empire.

market-reforms-of-alauddin-khalji.s: The market reforms of Alauddin Khalji were measures introduced by the sultan of Delhi in the early fourteenth century to control prices and supplies in the capital. Officials fixed prices for grain and other goods and enforced them strictly.

marrah-mountains.s: The Marrah Mountains, or Jebel Marra, are a volcanic massif in Darfur, in western Sudan. They were the homeland of the Fur people and the base from which Suleiman Solong founded the Darfur Sultanate in the seventeenth century.

marrakesh.s: Marrakesh is a city in Morocco founded by the Almoravids around 1070 as the capital of the Almoravid Empire. The Almohads captured it in 1147 and made it the capital of the Almohad Caliphate, adorning it with monuments such as the Koutoubia Mosque.

marwan-ii.s: Marwan II was the last Umayyad caliph, reigning from 744 until his death in 750. He came to power during civil wars and spent his reign fighting internal revolts.

marwanids.s: The Marwanids were the branch of the Umayyad family descended from Marwan I, who became caliph in 684. They ruled the Umayyad Caliphate from then until its fall in 750, and included caliphs such as Abd al-Malik.

marzban.s: A marzban was a Sasanian military governor responsible for a frontier province, or march, of the empire. Marzbans commanded troops and defended the borders, often holding considerable authority.

masekesa.s: Masekesa was a trading fair in the eastern Zimbabwe plateau region, in the area of Manica. According to the Rozvi Empire's profile, it was one of the coastal-linked markets where Portuguese and Swahili merchants bought gold and ivory in exchange for cloth, beads and…

mashafa-berha.s: The Mashafa Berha, or Book of Light, is a theological work attributed to the Ethiopian emperor Zara Yaqob in the fifteenth century. It set out church doctrine and religious regulations for the whole Ethiopian church.

mashhad.s: Mashhad is a city in north-eastern Iran, in Khorasan, and an important Shia pilgrimage centre around the shrine of Imam Reza. Nader Shah made it a principal seat of the Afsharid Empire.

mask-of-sargon.s: The Mask of Sargon is a copper alloy head of a ruler found at Nineveh, dating from the Akkadian period. It is often identified with Sargon of Akkad or Naram-Sin, though the identification is uncertain.

masmuda.s: The Masmuda were a Berber tribal confederation of the High Atlas and western Morocco. They provided the core support for Ibn Tumart's Almohad movement and its military forces.

massawa.s: Massawa is a port city on the Red Sea coast of present-day Eritrea. It was a key outlet for the Ethiopian Empire's trade, through which gold, ivory, slaves and aromatic resins were exported.

massina-jihad.s: The Massina jihad was a reformist Islamic movement led by Seku Amadu in the inner Niger delta, beginning in 1818. It established the Massina Caliphate, a theocratic state in present-day Mali.

masud-i-of-ghazni.s: Masud I was sultan of the Ghaznavid Empire, son and successor of Mahmud of Ghazni. He failed to contain the Seljuk Turks in Khorasan and was decisively defeated by them at the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040.

matchlock.s: The matchlock was an early firearm mechanism in which a slow-burning match was lowered onto the priming powder to fire the gun. Matchlock muskets spread across Eurasia in the sixteenth century.

matigan-i-hazar-datistan.s: The Matigan i Hazar Datistan, or Book of a Thousand Judgements, is a Middle Persian legal compilation from the late Sasanian period. It records legal decisions on matters such as contracts, property, family law and inheritance.

matope.s: Matope was an early ruler of the Mutapa Empire, successor of its founder Mutota, in the fifteenth century. He expanded the state significantly through conquest and alliances.

matopos-hills.s: The Matopos Hills, or Matobo Hills, are a granite landscape south of Bulawayo in present-day Zimbabwe. They were the centre of the Mwari religious cult, whose oracular shrines gave ritual legitimacy to the rulers of the Rozvi Empire.

matrilineal-descent.s: Matrilineal descent is a system in which kinship, inheritance and succession are traced through the mother's line. In the Ashanti Empire, membership of clans and succession to stools followed the matrilineal line.

matsuo-basho.s: Matsuo Basho was a Japanese poet of the seventeenth century, regarded as the greatest master of haiku. His works, including the travel journal The Narrow Road to the Deep North, combined poetry and prose.

matthew-c-perry.s: Matthew C. Perry was a United States naval officer who led an expedition to Japan in 1853 and 1854.

maurice-emperor.s: Maurice was a Byzantine emperor who reigned from 582 until 602. He helped restore Khosrow II to the Sasanian throne, securing peace with Persia.

mauritania.s: Mauritania is a country in north-west Africa, largely within the Sahara. Its southern region was part of the Ghana Empire, whose capital is identified with Koumbi Saleh in south-eastern Mauritania.

maurya-empire.s: The Maurya Empire was the first state to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE. Under Ashoka it reached its greatest extent, and Ashoka's edicts promoted dhamma and Buddhist ethics.

mawali.s: The mawali were non-Arab converts to Islam in the early caliphates, attached as clients to Arab tribes. Under the Umayyad Caliphate they often faced discrimination in taxation and status despite conversion.

maxim-gun.s: The Maxim gun was the first fully automatic machine gun, invented by Hiram Maxim in the 1880s. It gave European colonial forces overwhelming firepower over African armies.

maxtla.s: Maxtla was a Tepanec ruler of Azcapotzalco in the Valley of Mexico in the fifteenth century. After seizing power following his father Tezozomoc's death in 1426, he allegedly had the Mexica ruler murdered.

mayor-of-the-palace.s: The mayor of the palace was the chief official of the Merovingian Frankish kingdom. Over time the mayors became the real rulers while the Merovingian kings were reduced to figureheads.

mazandaran.s: Mazandaran is a province on the southern coast of the Caspian Sea in northern Iran. Its humid lowlands produced rice and silk, which was a major export of the Safavid Empire.

mbanza-kongo.s: Mbanza Kongo is a town in northern Angola, the capital of the Kingdom of Kongo. According to tradition it was founded by Lukeni lua Nimi.

mbata.s: Mbata was one of the provinces of the Kingdom of Kongo, lying in its eastern part. According to the Kongo Empire's profile, it was among the provinces, with Soyo and Nsundi, brought under the manikongo's authority by the late fifteenth century.

measles.s: Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. Introduced to the Americas by Europeans, it caused devastating epidemics among indigenous populations who had no immunity.

mecca.s: Mecca is a city in the Hejaz region of Arabia, the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and the holiest city of Islam. Pilgrimage to Mecca connected Muslim empires across the world, and rulers of the Mali, Songhai and Sokoto states made the journey.

mechanical-clock.s: A mechanical clock is a timekeeping device driven by a mechanism such as falling weights or water and an escapement. Chinese engineers built astronomical clock towers, such as Su Song's in the Song period, and the tradition continued under the Yuan Dynasty.

medang-kingdom.s: The Medang kingdom, also known as Mataram, was a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of central and later eastern Java from the eighth to the early eleventh century. It is associated with the building of monuments such as Borobudur and Prambanan.

medes.s: The Medes were an ancient Iranian people of north-western Iran. They formed the Median Empire, which joined with Babylon to destroy the Assyrian Empire in the late seventh century BCE.

media-atropatene.s: Media Atropatene was a kingdom in north-western Iran, roughly corresponding to present-day Iranian Azerbaijan. It was founded by Atropates after Alexander the Great's conquest and remained largely independent of the Seleucid Empire.

median-empire.s: The Median Empire was the state of the Medes in western Iran, which rose to power in the seventh century BCE. In alliance with Babylon, the Medes destroyed the Assyrian Empire, capturing Nineveh in 612 BCE.

medina.s: Medina is a city in the Hejaz region of Arabia, the second holiest city of Islam. The Prophet Muhammad migrated there in 622 and established the first Muslim community.

mediterranean.s: The Mediterranean Sea lies between southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It has been one of the great arenas of trade, migration and warfare throughout history.

medo-babylonian-alliance.s: The Medo-Babylonian alliance was the coalition between the Medes under Cyaxares and the Babylonians under Nabopolassar in the late seventh century BCE. Together they captured Nineveh in 612 BCE and destroyed the Assyrian Empire.

mehmed-ii.s: Mehmed II was an Ottoman sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire. Known as the Conqueror, he made the city the Ottoman capital and expanded the empire in the Balkans and Anatolia.

meiji-constitution.s: The Meiji Constitution was the constitution of the Empire of Japan, promulgated in 1889. Modelled partly on Prussian practice, it established a parliament, the Imperial Diet, while vesting supreme authority in the emperor.

meiji-restoration.s: The Meiji Restoration was the political revolution of 1868 that ended the Tokugawa Shogunate and restored direct imperial rule under Emperor Meiji. It launched a rapid programme of modernisation in government, industry and the military.

mekong-river.s: The Mekong is a major river of South-East Asia, flowing from Tibet through China, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. Its basin and floodplains supported rice agriculture and early states.

meluhha.s: Meluhha was a land known to ancient Mesopotamians, generally identified with the Indus Valley civilisation. It was reached by sea through the Persian Gulf and supplied goods such as carnelian, timber and other luxuries.

mema.s: Mema was a Soninke kingdom on the middle Niger in West Africa. According to the Mali Empire's profile, it was one of the forces in Sundiata Keita's coalition against Sumanguru of the Sosso.

menelik-ii.s: Menelik II was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 to 1913. He expanded and centralised the Ethiopian Empire and founded Addis Ababa as its capital.

mengistu-haile-mariam.s: Mengistu Haile Mariam was an Ethiopian army officer who rose to lead the Derg, the military council that overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974. The coup ended the Ethiopian Empire and the Solomonic monarchy.

mercantilism.s: Mercantilism was an economic doctrine dominant in early modern Europe, holding that national wealth depended on accumulating bullion and maintaining a favourable balance of trade. It encouraged state-sponsored trading companies, colonies and tariffs.

mercenary.s: A mercenary is a soldier who fights for pay in the service of a foreign power. Many empires relied on mercenaries, including the Achaemenid, Ptolemaic and Seleucid empires and above all Carthage, whose army was largely made up of hired troops.

mercenary-war.s: The Mercenary War was a revolt by Carthage's unpaid mercenary army and its Libyan subjects from 241 to 238 BCE, following the First Punic War. The rebellion threatened Carthage itself before it was crushed by Hamilcar Barca.

merchant-capitalism.s: Merchant capitalism is an early form of capitalism based on profit from trade rather than industrial production. Early modern Dutch and other merchants financed long-distance commerce in goods such as grain and timber.

meritocratic-recruitment.s: Meritocratic recruitment is the recurring practice of selecting officials or officers on the basis of ability rather than birth. The imperial examination system of the Han, Tang, Song and Ming dynasties is the classic example, while the Mongol Empire promoted commanders for…

meroe.s: Meroe was an ancient city on the east bank of the Nile in present-day Sudan, the capital of the Kushite Empire from around the sixth century BCE. It was a centre of iron production and trade, famous for its pyramids.

meroitic-script.s: The Meroitic script was the writing system of the Kingdom of Kush in its Meroitic period, used from about the second century BCE. It existed in hieroglyphic and cursive forms derived from Egyptian writing.

merovingian-dynasty.s: The Merovingian dynasty was the first royal house of the Franks, ruling from the fifth century until 751. Its founder Clovis I united much of Gaul and converted to Christianity.

merv.s: Merv was a great oasis city of Central Asia, in present-day Turkmenistan, on the Silk Road. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed near Merv in 651 while fleeing the Arab conquest.

mesoamerica.s: Mesoamerica is the cultural region of central and southern Mexico and northern Central America where civilisations such as the Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacan and the Aztecs developed. They shared features such as maize agriculture, calendars, writing and pyramid temples.

mesoamerican-codices.s: Mesoamerican codices are folding books painted on bark paper or deerskin by the peoples of Mesoamerica, recording history, religion, calendars and tribute. Many were destroyed by Spanish missionaries after the conquest of the Aztec Empire.

mesopotamia.s: Mesopotamia is the region between and around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, mainly in present-day Iraq. It was the setting of the earliest cities, writing and empires, including the Akkadian, Neo-Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian empires.

metsuke.s: Metsuke were inspectors or censors in the Tokugawa Shogunate who monitored officials, daimyo and samurai for misconduct or disloyalty. They reported to the shogunate's senior councils.

mexica.s: The Mexica were the Nahuatl-speaking people who founded Tenochtitlan on Lake Texcoco and led the Aztec Triple Alliance. They rose from mercenary service to dominance after defeating the Tepanecs in the fifteenth century.

mexico.s: Mexico is a country in North America whose central valley was the heartland of the Aztec Empire. After the Spanish conquest of 1519 to 1521, it became the core of the viceroyalty of New Spain, one of the richest parts of the Spanish Empire thanks to its silver mines.

mexico-city.s: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico, built on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan. After the Spanish conquest, Cortes deliberately razed the Aztec city and founded the new colonial capital on its site.

mfecane.s: The Mfecane was a period of widespread warfare, migration and state formation in southern Africa in the early nineteenth century, associated with the rise of the Zulu kingdom under Shaka. It sent waves of armed Nguni groups northwards across the Limpopo.

michael-viii-palaiologos.s: Michael VIII Palaiologos was a Byzantine emperor who reigned from 1259 to 1282 and founded the Palaiologan dynasty. In 1261 his forces recaptured Constantinople from the Latin Empire, restoring the Byzantine Empire.

middle-assyrian-empire.s: The Middle Assyrian Empire was the phase of Assyrian history that began when Ashur-uballit I asserted independence from Mitanni in the fourteenth century BCE. Assyria expanded across northern Mesopotamia and fought major rivals such as the Hittites and Babylon.

middle-east.s: The Middle East is the region of western Asia and north-eastern Africa including the Levant, Mesopotamia, Arabia, Iran, Anatolia and Egypt. It has been the setting of many empires, from the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates to the Seljuk, Safavid and Ottoman states.

middle-francia.s: Middle Francia was the central kingdom created by the Treaty of Verdun in 843, when the Carolingian Empire was divided among the sons of Louis the Pious. It went to Lothair I and stretched from the Low Countries through Burgundy to Italy.

migration-of-the-yuezhi.s: The migration of the Yuezhi was the westward movement of the Yuezhi people from the borders of China into Central Asia, driven by Xiongnu attacks around 176 BCE. They eventually settled in Bactria.

mihirakula.s: Mihirakula was a ruler of the Alchon Huns who controlled parts of north-western India in the early sixth century. He is remembered in Indian sources as a cruel persecutor of Buddhism.

milan.s: Milan is a major city of northern Italy, the capital of Lombardy. In the late Roman Empire it served as an imperial residence, and the Edict of Milan of 313 granted toleration to Christians.

military-colony.s: A military colony was a settlement of soldiers who farmed land in return for military service. The Han Dynasty established agricultural garrisons on its northern and western frontiers.

military-revolution.s: The military revolution is a historians' concept describing the transformation of European warfare in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries through firearms, new tactics and larger standing armies. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden is often seen as a central figure in it.

military-technological-disparity.s: Military technological disparity is the recurring pattern in which an empire is weakened or destroyed by opponents with superior weapons. Examples include the Sokoto Caliphate facing British Maxim guns, the Ashanti and Benin empires confronting European firearms, and the Wadai…

millenarianism.s: Millenarianism is the belief in a coming transformation of the world that will bring about a new age of justice and salvation. Millenarian movements often inspired popular uprisings in times of crisis.

millet.s: Millet is a group of hardy, drought-tolerant cereal grains grown widely in Africa and Asia. It was a staple crop of northern China under the Han and Ming dynasties and of the savannah and Sahel states of Africa, including the Songhai, Kanem-Bornu and Sokoto states.

millet-system.s: The millet system was the arrangement by which the Ottoman Empire organised its non-Muslim subjects into religious communities. Communities such as the Orthodox Christians, Armenians and Jews had considerable autonomy over religious, educational and legal matters under their…

mimar-sinan.s: Mimar Sinan was the chief architect of the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century, serving under Suleiman the Magnificent and his successors. He designed hundreds of buildings, including the Suleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne.

minas-gerais.s: Minas Gerais is a region of south-eastern Brazil. The discovery of gold there in the 1690s, followed by diamonds, produced a major revenue boom for the Portuguese Empire in the eighteenth century.

ming-empire.s: The Ming Empire was the Chinese dynasty founded by Zhu Yuanzhang in 1368 after the expulsion of the Yuan Dynasty. It rebuilt the Great Wall, launched the treasure voyages of Zheng He and became a centre of global silver trade.

ming-treasure-voyages.s: The Ming treasure voyages were seven large maritime expeditions led by the admiral Zheng He between 1405 and 1433. Huge fleets sailed through South-East Asia and the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and East Africa, displaying Ming power and collecting tribute.

minie-rifle.s: The Minie rifle was a muzzle-loading rifled musket firing a conical bullet that expanded into the barrel's rifling, allowing accurate long-range fire. It was widely used by British and French forces in the Crimean War.

mirwais-hotak.s: Mirwais Hotak was a Ghilzai Afghan chief from Kandahar who rebelled against Safavid rule in 1709. He killed the Safavid governor and established an independent Afghan state.

mise-en-valeur.s: Mise en valeur, meaning 'development' or 'making productive', was a French colonial doctrine calling for the economic exploitation and development of colonies. It was associated particularly with the minister Albert Sarraut in the early twentieth century.

misl.s: A misl was one of the Sikh confederacies that controlled parts of the Punjab in the eighteenth century, each led by a chief. Among them were the Sukerchakia and Bhangi misls.

missi-dominici.s: The missi dominici, 'envoys of the lord', were officials sent by Charlemagne to supervise local administration across the Carolingian Empire. Usually travelling in pairs of a churchman and a layman, they checked on counts, heard complaints and announced royal decrees.

mission-civilisatrice.s: The mission civilisatrice, or civilising mission, was the ideology used to justify French colonial rule. It claimed that France had a duty to spread its language, culture and values to colonised peoples.

mississippi-river.s: The Mississippi is the principal river of North America, draining a vast basin into the Gulf of Mexico. French explorers travelled it in the seventeenth century and claimed its basin as Louisiana for the French Empire.

mita.s: The mita was a system of compulsory labour in the Andes, adapted by the Spanish Empire from an Inca institution. Indigenous communities had to send a share of their men to work in mines, notably the silver mines of Potosi, and other enterprises.

mitanni.s: Mitanni was a Hurrian-speaking kingdom in northern Mesopotamia and Syria, powerful from about the sixteenth to the fourteenth century BCE. It was a rival and later ally of the Egyptian New Kingdom and dominated Assyria.

mithridates-i-of-parthia.s: Mithridates I was king of Parthia from about 171 to 132 BCE and is regarded as the founder of the Parthian Empire as a major power. He conquered Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucid Empire.

mixed-constitution.s: A mixed constitution is a form of government combining elements of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy, so that each checks the others. Ancient writers such as Aristotle and Polybius praised Carthage for such a constitution.

mobedan-mobed.s: The mobedan mobed, 'priest of priests', was the chief Zoroastrian priest of the Sasanian Empire. He headed the religious hierarchy and had important judicial and advisory functions.

moctezuma-ii.s: Moctezuma II was ruler of the Aztec Empire from 1502 to 1520. He expanded the empire and centralised power, but faced the arrival of Hernan Cortes in 1519.

moderating-power.s: The moderating power, Poder Moderador, was a constitutional power given to the emperor of Brazil by the constitution of 1824. It allowed him to appoint and dismiss ministries, dissolve the chamber and act as arbiter among the branches of government.

modernism.s: Modernism was an artistic and cultural movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries that broke with traditional forms. According to the Benin Empire's profile, the Benin bronzes looted in 1897 influenced European modernism through the admiration of artists…

modest-mussorgsky.s: Modest Mussorgsky was a nineteenth-century Russian composer, known for works such as the opera Boris Godunov and Pictures at an Exhibition. He belonged to a group of composers who sought a distinctively Russian national music.

modu-chanyu.s: Modu Chanyu was ruler of the Xiongnu from 209 to 174 BCE and founder of the Xiongnu Empire as a unified steppe power. He defeated the Donghu and the Yuezhi and inflicted a heavy defeat on the Han founder Liu Bang at Baideng in 200 BCE.

moghulistan.s: Moghulistan was the eastern successor state of the Chagatai Empire, based on the Tarim Basin and the Ili River steppe. After the Timurid conquest of Transoxiana in the fourteenth century, it remained the surviving Chagataid realm.

mohammed-al-fadl.s: Mohammed al-Fadl was a sultan of Darfur in the early nineteenth century. The traveller Muhammad al-Tunisi lived at his court between about 1803 and 1812 and recorded a prosperous court and a sophisticated commercial network.

mohammed-tayrab.s: Mohammed Tayrab was a sultan of Darfur in the eighteenth century. He campaigned eastward and annexed Kordofan in the 1780s, roughly doubling the Darfur Sultanate's territory.

mongke.s: Mongke was Great Khan of the Mongol Empire from 1251 to 1259, a grandson of Genghis Khan. He sent his brother Hulagu to the Middle East, leading to the foundation of the Ilkhanate, and his brother Kublai against the Song.

mongol-conquest-of-dali.s: The Mongol conquest of Dali was the campaign of 1253 in which Mongol forces under Kublai overran the kingdom of Dali in present-day Yunnan. The conquest outflanked the Song Dynasty from the south-west.

mongol-conquest-of-the-jin-dynasty.n: Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty
mongol-conquest-of-the-jin-dynasty.s: The Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty was the series of campaigns from 1211 in which Genghis Khan and his successors destroyed the Jurchen Jin state in northern China. The Jin capital Zhongdu fell in 1215, and the dynasty ended in 1234.

mongol-conquest-of-the-song-dynasty.n: Mongol conquest of the Song dynasty
mongol-conquest-of-the-song-dynasty.s: The Mongol conquest of the Song Dynasty was a long series of campaigns from 1235 to 1279. Song resistance was strong, with river defences and fortified cities such as Xiangyang holding out for years.

mongol-empire.s: The Mongol Empire was founded by Genghis Khan in 1206 and became the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to eastern Europe. Its conquests destroyed states such as the Khwarazmian Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate.

mongol-invasion-of-central-asia.s: The Mongol invasion of Central Asia was Genghis Khan's campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire, which devastated the cities of Transoxiana and Khorasan around 1220. Cities such as Bukhara and Samarkand were captured and many populations massacred.

mongol-invasion-of-java.s: The Mongol invasion of Java was a naval expedition sent by Kublai Khan of the Yuan Dynasty in 1292 to 1293. The Javanese prince Raden Wijaya used the Mongol force against his rival and then turned on the invaders, driving them out.

mongol-invasion-of-the-khwarazmian-empir.n: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
mongol-invasion-of-the-khwarazmian-empir.s: The Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire was the campaign of 1219 to 1221 launched by Genghis Khan after the Khwarazm Shah's governor killed Mongol envoys and merchants. Mongol armies captured and devastated the great cities of Transoxiana and Khorasan.

mongol-invasion-of-the-levant.s: The Mongol invasion of the Levant was the campaign of 1258 to 1260 in which Hulagu's forces, after sacking Baghdad, invaded Syria. They captured Aleppo and Damascus, ending the remaining Ayyubid principalities there.

mongol-invasions-of-india.s: The Mongol invasions of India were a series of attacks on the Delhi Sultanate by Mongols of the Chagatai realm, peaking between 1297 and 1306. Alauddin Khalji repeatedly repelled them, protecting northern India from the devastation suffered elsewhere.

mongol-invasions-of-japan.s: The Mongol invasions of Japan were two attempts by Kublai Khan's Yuan Dynasty to conquer Japan, in 1274 and 1281. Both were defeated by Japanese defenders and by storms that wrecked the invasion fleets, remembered as the kamikaze or divine winds.

mongolia.s: Mongolia is a region of steppe, mountains and desert in north-east Asia. It was the homeland of successive nomadic empires, including the Xiongnu Empire, the Gokturk Empire and the Mongol Empire.

mongols.s: The Mongols are a nomadic people of the Mongolian steppe who were united under Genghis Khan in 1206. Their conquests created the Mongol Empire and reshaped Eurasia, destroying states such as the Khwarazmian Empire and the Song Dynasty and threatening the Ayyubid and Mamluk…

monotheism.s: Monotheism is the belief in a single god. The Assyrian Empire's profile notes that the Assyrian deportation of the population of the Kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE, and the experience of exile more broadly, contributed to the reconception of the God of Israel as a universal…

monsoon.s: The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds that brings heavy summer rains to South and South-East Asia. Monsoon rains governed agriculture and seaborne trade across the region.

moravia.s: Moravia is a historical region in the eastern part of the present-day Czech Republic. It was a crown land of the Habsburg monarchy and part of the Austrian half of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

moriscos.s: The Moriscos were Muslims of Spain who had been forcibly converted to Christianity and were eventually expelled in the early seventeenth century. Many settled in North Africa.

moroccan-invasion-of-songhai.s: The Moroccan invasion of Songhai was the expedition sent across the Sahara in 1591 by Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco under the command of Judar Pasha. His force of about 4,000 men, armed with firearms, defeated the much larger Songhai army at the Battle of Tondibi.

morocco.s: Morocco is a country in north-west Africa with Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts. It was the heartland of the Almoravid Empire and the Almohad Caliphate, whose capital was Marrakesh.

moscow.s: Moscow is the capital of Russia, which grew from a minor principality into the centre of the Russian state. Polish-Lithuanian forces occupied Moscow during the Time of Troubles in the early seventeenth century.

mossi.s: The Mossi are a people of present-day Burkina Faso, who founded a group of kingdoms in the Volta basin from the fifteenth century. Mossi cavalry raided northwards into the Niger bend.

mosul.s: Mosul is a city on the Tigris in northern Iraq, opposite the ruins of ancient Nineveh. In the twelfth century it was a base of the Zengid dynasty, in whose service Saladin and his family rose to power.

mount-ararat.s: Mount Ararat is a high volcanic mountain in eastern Anatolia, near the borders of present-day Turkey, Armenia and Iran. The surrounding region had a large Armenian population.

mount-mahendraparvata.s: Mount Mahendraparvata is a sacred mountain plateau in Cambodia, now known as Phnom Kulen. In 802 CE Jayavarman II performed a consecration ritual there, declaring himself universal monarch and freeing the region from Javanese overlordship.

mounted-archer.s: A mounted archer is a cavalry soldier who shoots arrows from horseback. Mounted archers were the foundation of steppe military power, combining mobility with firepower.

mouseion.s: The Mouseion was a research institution founded in Alexandria under the early Ptolemaic kings, dedicated to the Muses. It housed scholars and scientists supported by the state and was closely linked to the Library of Alexandria.

movable-type.s: Movable type is a printing system using individual, reusable characters that can be arranged to form texts. It was invented in China by Bi Sheng in the eleventh century under the Song Dynasty, using ceramic type.

mozambique.s: Mozambique is a country on the coast of south-eastern Africa. The Portuguese established trading posts on its coast from the early sixteenth century and pushed inland along the Zambezi, interacting with and undermining the Mutapa Empire.

muawiya-i.s: Muawiya I was the founder of the Umayyad Caliphate, ruling from 661 to 680. As governor of Syria he opposed the caliph Ali in the first Muslim civil war, and after Ali's death he became caliph, ending the Rashidun Caliphate.

mughal-empire.s: The Mughal Empire was a dynasty of Timurid descent that ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from 1526, when Babur defeated the Lodi sultan at Panipat. Under Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb it became one of the richest states in the world.

mughan-assembly.s: The Mughan assembly was the great gathering held on the Mughan plain in 1736 at which Nader Afshar was proclaimed shah. Nader formally deposed the infant Safavid Abbas III, ending the Safavid dynasty and founding the Afsharid Empire.

mughan-plain.s: The Mughan plain is a lowland steppe south of the Aras river, divided today between Azerbaijan and Iran. It was a traditional pasture and gathering place for armies and tribes.

muhammad-al-nasir.s: Muhammad al-Nasir was Almohad caliph from 1199 to 1213, son of Yaqub al-Mansur. He faced a coalition of Christian Iberian kingdoms and was decisively defeated at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, after which he fled.

muhammad-al-sharif-of-wadai.s: Muhammad al-Sharif was sultan of Wadai from 1835 to 1858. His reign was the Wadai Empire's last period of sustained expansion and internal consolidation.

muhammad-al-tunisi.s: Muhammad al-Tunisi was a North African scholar and traveller who lived at the court of the Darfur Sultanate from about 1803 to 1812, under Sultan Mohammed al-Fadl. His account of Darfur's society, commerce and court is one of the most important sources on the sultanate.

muhammad-baqir-majlesi.s: Muhammad Baqir Majlesi was a leading Shia cleric of the late Safavid Empire. He was an influential theologian who compiled the vast collection of hadith known as the Bihar al-Anwar.

muhammad-bello.s: Muhammad Bello was the son of Usman dan Fodio and the first sultan of Sokoto, ruling from 1817 to 1837. He was one of the leaders of his father's jihad and founded the city of Sokoto.

muhammad-bin-tughlaq.s: Muhammad bin Tughlaq was sultan of Delhi from 1325 to 1351, known for ambitious but unsuccessful schemes. These included moving the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad and introducing token copper currency, which led to widespread forgery.

muhammad-ibn-ibrahim-al-fazari.s: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Fazari was an astronomer of the early Abbasid period. Writing around 777 CE, he gave one of the earliest written references to the Ghana Empire, describing it as the land of gold.

muhammad-ibn-nasir.s: Muhammad ibn Nasir was a ruler of the Adal Sultanate in the late sixteenth century. He was killed at the Battle of the Webi River in a campaign against the Ethiopian Empire.

muhammad-ibn-qasim.s: Muhammad ibn Qasim was an Umayyad general who conquered Sind in the lower Indus valley around 711 to 712. His campaign brought Islam and Umayyad rule to part of the Indian subcontinent.

muhammad-of-ghor.s: Muhammad of Ghor was a ruler of the Ghurid dynasty who conquered much of northern India in the late twelfth century. His victory at the second Battle of Tarain in 1192 opened the Ganges plain to Muslim rule.

muhammad-shaybani.s: Muhammad Shaybani was the leader of the Uzbeks who conquered Transoxiana and Khorasan in the early sixteenth century. He drove the Timurids from Samarkand and Herat, ending the Timurid Empire.

muhammad-v-of-adal.s: Muhammad V was a sultan of Adal in the late sixteenth century. He was defeated by the Ethiopian emperor Sarsa Dengel and executed in 1577.

muhammadu-attahiru-i.s: Muhammadu Attahiru I was the last independent sultan of Sokoto. When the British conquered the Sokoto Caliphate in 1903, he refused to submit and led his followers eastward in a hijra recalling Usman dan Fodio's migration.

mukden-incident.s: The Mukden Incident was a staged explosion on a Japanese-owned railway near Mukden in Manchuria in 1931. Officers of the Kwantung Army used it as a pretext to occupy Manchuria without authorisation from Tokyo.

mukombwe.s: Mukombwe was a ruler of the Mutapa state in the seventeenth century. According to the Rozvi Empire's profile, he granted Changamire Dombo I extensive herds and regional authority in the Guruuswa province around 1670.

mulopwe.s: Mulopwe was the title of the sacred king of the Luba Empire. The mulopwe was believed to possess a special royal essence, balopwe, which legitimated his rule.

multan.s: Multan is an ancient city in the southern Punjab, in present-day Pakistan. Ranjit Singh captured it in 1818, extending the Sikh Empire.

multi-ethnic-integration.s: Multi-ethnic integration is the recurring pattern by which empires incorporated diverse peoples into their armies, administrations and elites. The Abbasid Caliphate drew on Persians, Arabs and Turks, the Tang Dynasty employed Turkic and Sogdian commanders, and the Ottoman…

munzo.s: Munzo was the site of the royal court established by Kalala Ilunga, the founder of the Luba Empire. According to the Luba profile, from Munzo he expanded Luba territory in several directions.

muqan-qaghan.s: Muqan Qaghan was ruler of the Gokturk Empire from 553 to 572. Under him the empire expanded dramatically, exterminating the remaining Rouran and defeating the Khitans.

muqarnas.s: Muqarnas is a form of architectural ornament in Islamic architecture consisting of tiers of small niches, creating a honeycomb or stalactite effect in vaults and domes. It became a defining feature of Seljuk architecture.

muqattam-hill.s: The Muqattam Hill is a range of hills on the eastern edge of Cairo. Saladin built the Cairo Citadel on a spur of the Muqattam, overlooking the city.

muqti.s: A muqti was a holder of an iqta, a revenue assignment granted to military officers in medieval Islamic states. In the Seljuk Empire, muqtis acted as provincial military governors, collecting revenue from their assignments to support troops.

murcia.s: Murcia is a city in south-eastern Spain that formed part of al-Andalus during the medieval Islamic period. Its irrigated huertas, sustained by hydraulic techniques inherited and developed by Arab cultivators, produced substantial agricultural surpluses.

mursili-i.s: Mursili I was an early king of the Hittites, remembered for his long-distance raid down the Euphrates around 1595 BCE. The campaign sacked Babylon, carried off the statues of Marduk and his consort, and ended the First Babylonian Dynasty.

musaylima.s: Musaylima was a seventh-century Arabian leader of the Banu Hanifa who claimed prophethood and led one of the main challenges to Medinan authority after the death of Muhammad. He was killed at the Battle of Yamama during the Ridda Wars of 632–633 CE.

muscat.s: Muscat is a port city on the coast of Oman, commanding sea routes between the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea. Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire conquered it in about 1743, extending Iranian commercial and naval reach.

musi-river.s: The Musi River is a river in southern Sumatra on which the city of Palembang stands. Palembang served as the core capital of the Srivijaya Empire, and its riverine position allowed the state to oversee shipping between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea through the…

musket.s: The musket is a muzzle-loading, smoothbore firearm that became the standard infantry weapon in many armies from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century. Its spread transformed warfare across Eurasia and Africa.

muslim-conquest-of-the-levant-and-egypt.n: Muslim conquest of the Levant and Egypt
muslim-conquest-of-the-levant-and-egypt.s: The Muslim conquest of the Levant and Egypt refers to the Arab campaigns that took Syria, Palestine and Egypt from Byzantine control in the seventh century. The site's Byzantine Empire profile dates the loss of Egypt and Syria to 637–642 CE and describes it as the empire's…

mustafa-kemal-ataturk.s: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was an Ottoman army officer who led the Turkish national movement after the First World War and became the founding president of the Republic of Turkey. Following the Ottoman defeat and the Allied occupation of Istanbul, his forces resisted the post-war…

mustansirite-hardship.s: The Mustansirite Hardship was a prolonged crisis in Fatimid Egypt from 1064 to 1071, caused by seven consecutive years of catastrophically low Nile floods. According to the site's Fatimid Caliphate profile, it killed an estimated 40,000 people, halved Cairo's population and…

mutapa-empire.s: The Mutapa Empire, also known as the Mwene Mutapa state, was a Shona kingdom that emerged in the mid-fifteenth century between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, in present-day Zimbabwe and Mozambique. Founded by Nyatsimba Mutota, it controlled gold, salt and trade routes linking…

mutazilism.s: Mu'tazilism was a school of Islamic theology that emphasised reason and rational argument in interpreting doctrine, including the view that the Quran was created rather than eternal. Under Caliph al-Ma'mun it was adopted as state doctrine, asserting the caliph's right to…

muwatalli-ii.s: Muwatalli II was a king of the Hittite Empire in the early thirteenth century BCE. He commanded the Hittite forces against Ramesses II of Egypt at the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE, one of the largest chariot battles of the ancient world.

mwaant-yaav.s: Mwaant Yaav (also written Mwata Yamvo) is the title of the paramount ruler of the Lunda Empire in central Africa, taken by each king from the late seventeenth century onwards. The Mwaant Yaav and the nobility controlled the trade in salt, copper and ivory and received tribute…

mwaant-yaav-i.s: Mwaant Yaav I was a ruler of the Lunda Empire in central Africa, associated with the period c. 1665–1700.

mwari-cult.s: The Mwari cult is a Shona religious tradition centred on the high god Mwari, with oracular shrines in the Matopos Hills of present-day Zimbabwe. In the Rozvi Empire it provided ritual sanction and ideological legitimacy for the Changamire rulers.

mwene-mutapa.s: Mwene Mutapa was the title of the king of the Mutapa Empire, a term from which the state itself took its name. The ruler stood at the apex of a hierarchy of nobles, spirit mediums and commoners.

myrrh.s: Myrrh is an aromatic resin obtained from trees native to north-east Africa and southern Arabia, prized in antiquity for incense, perfume and embalming. In the Egyptian New Kingdom it was a key import from the land of Punt.

mzilikazi.s: Mzilikazi was a nineteenth-century military leader who founded the Ndebele kingdom in south-western Zimbabwe. His Ndebele moved onto the plateau from the south around 1840, completing the occupation of the former Rozvi heartland.
